analysis.one_liner: Channels Year 2000 computer-failure lawsuits into mandatory arbitration and caps the damages companies must pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill set special rules for lawsuits over computer breakdowns caused by the Year 2000 date bug. It sent every such complaint to mandatory arbitration before a court would hear it, capped payouts for pain and suffering at the amount of medical bills, limited punitive damages, shielded corporate directors and officers from most liability, and gave people only two years after January 1, 2000 to sue. Despite its name, its main effect would have been to limit how much companies had to pay when their software or systems failed on Y2K.
analysis.who_benefits: Software and computer vendors, corporate directors and officers, and insurers facing a wave of Y2K lawsuits. The bill required that the defendant's unreasonableness be shown 'as an end user' (someone using the software or hardware), capped compensable pain and suffering at medical expenses, capped punitive damages at three times actual damages and only for willful conduct proven by clear and convincing evidence, and protected directors unless they failed to exercise due diligence [S3]. Claimants would still get a defined path to recover for personal injury, wrongful death, and property damage including lost profits, but on the bill's terms [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Created a uniform federal framework letting claimants recover for personal injury, wrongful death, and property damage (including lost profits and repair costs) caused by a Y2K failure, upon a preponderance-of-the-evidence showing that the failure caused a foreseeable loss, the defendant acted unreasonably, and the loss was proximately caused by the defendant [S2][S3].
Allowed punitive damages for willful and wanton conduct, up to three times actual damages, and excluded government regulatory and enforcement actions from the bill's rules [S2][S3].
Left actions arising out of express written contracts — such as software licenses with warranty terms — outside the bill's special procedures, so those claims kept ordinary contract law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People and businesses injured by Y2K failures. Their complaints would be referred automatically to arbitration rather than decided by a judge or jury, their pain-and-suffering awards capped at medical and hospital expenses, their punitive damages capped and hard to obtain, their claims against corporate officers largely barred, and their window to sue closed two years after January 1, 2000 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: People and firms injured by Y2K failures

drawbacks.text: Pain and suffering could not exceed the amount of medical and hospital expenses, a cap that compensates someone with high medical bills far more generously than someone whose injury was painful but cheap to treat [S3].

Punitive damages were available only for willful and wanton conduct proven by clear and convincing evidence, capped at three times actual damages, and unavailable in property-damage-only cases — a much higher bar than ordinary tort law [S2][S3].
Every Y2K damages complaint would be referred by the court clerk to mandatory arbitration, taking the decision away from judges and juries and adding a layer of cost and delay for claimants [S2][S3].

The proof standard required the defendant's action or inaction 'as an end user' to be unreasonable, and directors and officers were responsible only for failure to exercise due diligence — language that would make claims against the companies that made and sold faulty software harder to sustain [S2][S3].
A two-year statute of limitations running from January 1, 2000 gave claimants little time to discover and pursue injuries from failures that might surface slowly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered claimants a real recovery framework, including injury and death damages, but the architecture around it — mandatory arbitration, a pain-and-suffering cap tied to medical bills, a high bar for punitive damages, a director shield, and a short filing window — tilted the system toward defendants. A consumer hurt by a Y2K failure would have given up a jury trial and substantial damages in exchange for a faster, more predictable process. The bill's consumer-friendly title promised more than its liability-limiting provisions delivered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the entire two years of the 106th Congress without a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Manzullo introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, 'for himself, Mr. DeLay, and Mr. Dreier,' and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S3][S5].
Nine Republican members cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote [S1][S5].
The bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, anyone with a Year 2000 claim — consumers and businesses alike — kept the ordinary rules of their state and federal courts, with access to juries and uncapped damages under existing law, and the software and insurance industries never got the liability limits the bill would have provided.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call exists to show where the full chamber stood.

industries.note: Vendors faced potentially enormous Y2K liability exposure. The bill's proof standard keyed to the defendant's conduct 'as an end user,' its damage caps, and its two-year filing window would have shrunk what injured customers could recover from the companies that built and sold failing systems [S2][S3].

The bill made directors and officers responsible only if they failed to exercise due diligence in overseeing the acts cited by a plaintiff, shielding them from ordinary personal liability for Y2K failures at companies they oversaw [S2][S3].
Caps on pain-and-suffering awards (tied to medical expenses) and punitive damages directly reduce the payouts insurers would owe on Y2K injury claims [S3].

By directing court clerks to refer every Y2K damages complaint to mandatory arbitration, the bill would have made arbitration the required first stop for this entire category of disputes, creating a guaranteed volume of cases for arbitration providers [S2][S3].
